events.description: Recovering the northeast in 1356 brought into Goryeo's service Yi Ja-chun, a frontier Korean lord who had served the Mongols as a local official in the amputated territory, and his son Yi Seong-gye — the family that would end the dynasty thirty-six years later.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yi Ja-chun's Mongolian name was Wulusibuhua, reflecting his decades of service under Yuan administration. He had been a minor military officer of the Yuan Empire before switching allegiance to Goryeo when Gongmin's army arrived. Yi Seong-gye was around seventeen when his family changed sides, beginning a military career on the Goryeo frontier that would make him the most powerful general of his age.

events.label: The Red Turbans Invade
events.description: Red Turban rebels — Chinese peasant fighters driven by a millenarian creed and smashed by the Yuan — spilled across the border into Korea in two invasions (1359, 1361); in 1361 they sacked the capital Kaesong itself and Gongmin fled the length of the country to Andong before Goryeo's generals could retake the city.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Red Turbans were one branch of a broad anti-Yuan movement; another branch would eventually produce the founder of the Ming dynasty, making this the same revolutionary wave that ended Mongol rule in China. The invaders numbered in the tens of thousands and crossed the frozen Yalu into Goryeo. After retaking the capital, Goryeo executed the generals it blamed for the initial failure — internal recrimination on top of the invasion itself.

events.label: Sin Don's Rise
events.description: Shattered by his queen's death in childbirth in 1365, Gongmin withdrew from normal governance and elevated Sin Don — a low-born Buddhist monk with no clan, no estates, and therefore nothing personal to lose from attacking the great families — to the rank of royal preceptor and near-total chief minister.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sin Don's Dharma name was P'yŏnjo. His lack of aristocratic lineage was precisely his qualification: every other potential reformer had family land and clan ties that made real redistribution politically impossible. The aristocracy could not beat his rulings in court, so they worked on the king directly — feeding Gongmin accusations of corruption, lechery, and plots against the throne for years until his trust curdled. Sin Don was purged and executed in 1371, a textbook case of how entrenched elites destroyed reformers not in the field but in the ruler's ear.

events.label: The Land and Slave Reform
events.description: In 1366 Sin Don ran the Jeonmin Byeonjeong Dogam (a Directorate for the Reclassification of Land and People), which returned illegally seized estates to their original owners and freed people who had been illegally enslaved — wildly popular among the poor, a declaration of war on the aristocracy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The directorate's name translates roughly to 'Office for Rectifying Fields and People' — 'people' here meaning those wrongly reduced to slave or serf status by powerful families seizing their lands. This was the same structural problem Goryeo had tried to fix with the Jeonsigwa land reforms as far back as Chapter 2: great families used political power to absorb peasant land, shrinking the tax base and growing a near-landless underclass. Sin Don's directorate was the most aggressive attempt yet, and it still failed — not because the policy was wrong but because the king who backed it could be manipulated.

events.label: Gongmin Assassinated
events.description: Sin Don was purged and executed in 1371; three years later Gongmin was murdered by his own palace attendants. The dynasty's last serious attempt at top-down reform had collapsed, and the men who would actually change Korea were now soldiers, not ministers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gongmin had no legitimate heir — the boy put forward as his successor, King U, was widely rumored not to be his biological son. His murder by palace attendants suggests the plot came from within the court circle rather than from the great clans directly, though the nobles who had fought Sin Don's reforms had every reason to want the unstable reformist king gone. The assassination left Goryeo with a weak boy-king and no reform agenda, clearing the field for the military men.

events.label: Choe Yeong Beats Back the Pirates
events.description: Japanese wokou (WOH-koh) pirate fleets — actually a mixed sea-economy of Japanese, Korean, and Chinese raiders — hammered the Korean coast with mounting scale from the 1350s onward, sailing up rivers and sacking inland towns; the incorruptible general Choe Yeong's victory at Hongsan in 1376 made him the dynasty's military conscience.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Choe Yeong's famous maxim came from his father's deathbed: 'regard gold as you would a stone' — a charge against corruption that Choe was said to have honored for his entire career, and which Koreans quoted for centuries. He had also fought in the Red Turban campaigns and against the Yuan, making him the last of Goryeo's old-guard generals. He was ultimately executed by Yi Seong-gye after the Wihwado coup — the man whose dynasty ended him had once served under him.

events.label: The Jikji: Movable Metal Type
events.description: In 1377 monks at Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju printed the Jikji (JEEK-jee), an anthology of Buddhist teachings, using movable metal type — making it the oldest book printed with movable metal type that survives anywhere in the world, 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: UNESCO inscribed the Jikji on the Memory of the World Register in September 2001, confirming its status as the world's oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type. The surviving volume is the second of two and sits today in the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris — brought to France in the nineteenth century and not repatriated. Metal movable type had first been recorded in Korea in 1234 on Ganghwa Island (Chapter 6), making the Jikji the flowering of a 143-year-old Korean technology.

events.label: Choe Mu-seon's Gunpowder Bureau
events.description: Official Choe Mu-seon (cheh moo-SUN) obtained the Chinese formula for refining saltpeter — by tradition by hosting a merchant for a year until he revealed the secret — and persuaded the court to found a Firearms Directorate in 1377, producing Korea's first cannon specifically to destroy the pirate fleets.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Choe Mu-seon was unusual in being a civilian official who became a military inventor — the gunpowder program was his personal crusade, not a standing military project. Song China had fielded gunpowder weapons since roughly the eleventh century; Goryeo's near-century gap as first a Mongol enemy then a Mongol vassal had frozen its military technology at exactly the moment gunpowder warfare was transforming Asia. Choe went on to design multiple gunpowder-based weapons beyond cannon — rockets, fire arrows — that Korea would use for generations.

events.label: Cannon at Jinpo, Slaughter at Hwangsan
events.description: In 1380 Choe Mu-seon's new cannon destroyed a large wokou fleet at the mouth of the Geum River at Jinpo; the pirates who made it ashore were then annihilated by Yi Seong-gye at the Battle of Hwangsan — the twin victories that turned a frontier commander into a national hero with a devoted army.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Jinpo battle is believed to have been among the first large-scale uses of Korean cannon in naval combat. Yi Seong-gye's Hwangsan campaign involved a pursuit deep into inland Jeolla province — the wokou had been bold enough to penetrate far from the coast. His victory there gave him the kind of nationwide prestige that a frontier general, however effective, could not normally acquire; it was Hwangsan that made him a figure every Goryeo subject knew by name.

events.label: The Wihwa Island Turnaround
events.description: In 1388 Yi Seong-gye was ordered to invade Ming-held Liaodong across the Yalu; judging the war suicidal, he marched to Wihwa Island (WEE-hwah) in the river, turned his army around, marched back on the capital, seized the government, and had Choe Yeong executed — the pivot point that ended Goryeo.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yi Seong-gye articulated four reasons against the invasion that became famous: a small country should not attack a large one; summer campaigns in the south were a bad time to march north; with the country mobilized, the Japanese pirates would raid the undefended rear; and the rainy season would rot the bows and spread disease among the soldiers. He was right on every count. The coup he staged is specifically called a 'retreat,' not a rebellion, because he framed the turn-back as responsible leadership — Heaven withdrawing its favor from a government ordering pointless war.

events.label: The Gwajeon Land Law
events.description: In 1391 Yi Seong-gye and the radical Neo-Confucians enacted the Gwajeon Law: the old land registers were burned in a public fire in the capital, and revenue rights were redistributed — gutting the great aristocratic estates and funding the new regime, destroying in a single act the economic foundation of the class being replaced.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The burning of the registers was deliberately theatrical — a public, irreversible demonstration that the old order was gone. The Gwajeon system replaced the Jeonsigwa (the land-revenue system running since Chapter 2), which had been failing for centuries as noble families absorbed land meant to fund state officials. The new law granted revenue rights only to current officeholders, not as hereditary property — meaning the aristocracy's land wealth could not be passed to children, breaking the dynastic cycle that had rotted Goryeo from within.

events.label: Jeong Mong-ju Murdered; Joseon Founded
events.description: When the loyalist scholar Jeong Mong-ju refused to abandon Goryeo, Yi Seong-gye's son Yi Bang-won had him clubbed to death with an iron mace on Seonjuk Bridge in spring 1392; months later Yi Seong-gye accepted the throne as Taejo — taking the same founder's temple name Wang Geon had used 474 years before — and named his dynasty Joseon.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jeong Mong-ju was Yi Seong-gye's personal friend and had fought alongside him in the anti-pirate campaigns — his murder was not the removal of an enemy but the destruction of a loyal comrade who would not turn. The tradition that a bloodstain rose on Seonjuk Bridge stones whenever it rained became one of the most enduring legends in Korean memory. Taejo abdicated just six years after taking the throne during a succession struggle among his sons; one of the sons who fought that war was Yi Bang-won, the very man who killed Jeong Mong-ju.

events.label: Jeong Do-jeon and the New Order
events.description: The revolutionary Neo-Confucian Jeong Do-jeon, who had argued a dynasty losing the people's trust forfeits the right to rule, became the architect of the Joseon state — Goryeo's afterlife was its replacement.
